title: Grant's Terms at Appomattox
text:
On April 9, 1865, after four years of war and a final week of retreat, Robert E. Lee met Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of Wilmer McLean's house at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, to surrender the Army of Northern Virginia.

Grant wrote the terms himself, at a small table. In his Personal Memoirs he says he did not know what he would write until he began. The officers and men were to be paroled, give their word not to fight again, and go home, not to be disturbed by United States authority as long as they kept their parole and obeyed the laws. Officers could keep their side arms, horses and baggage. When Lee mentioned that many of his cavalrymen and gunners owned their horses, Grant agreed that any man claiming a horse or mule could take it home to work his farm. He also arranged rations for Lee's hungry soldiers.

When Union troops began firing salutes to celebrate, Grant ordered them stopped. He wrote that the Confederates were now their prisoners and that he did not want to exult over their downfall. Lee told Grant the terms would have a very happy effect on his army.
lesson: When you win, how you treat the people who lost shapes everything that follows. Generosity at the right moment costs little and builds peace.
people: Ulysses S. Grant, Robert E. Lee
source: Ulysses S. Grant, Personal Memoirs, chapter 67; Grant's letter of terms to Lee, April 9, 1865
